title: The dog-walking business
scenario:
Sam runs a small dog-walking business in their town. Sam uses a chat app for four jobs this month:

1. A job ad for a second dog walker.
2. The reviews page of the new website.
3. A short blog post on how much walking a dog needs.
4. An email to a customer with next month's price.

Sam asks you to help them stay fair and honest.

questions.prompt: The app's job ad says: "We want a young, energetic guy who loves dogs." What should Sam do?

options.text: Post it as it is, because the app learned the words from many real job ads.
options.explanation: Learning from real text is how bias gets in. The OpenAI docs list bias among the known limits of language models, so a fluent draft can still leave people out.

options.text: Change "guy" to "person" and keep "young", because only gender is a problem here.
options.explanation: Age is a bias too. The Google AI docs list age among the kinds of bias that models are tested for. The line still shuts out older walkers who can do the job.

options.text: Rewrite it to describe the work itself, like long walks in any weather, not age or gender.
options.explanation: Right. The line picks people by age and gender, not by the job. Describe what the work needs, and anyone who can do it can apply.

options.text: Ask the app if the ad is fair, and post it if the app says that it is.
options.explanation: The app wrote the biased line, so its yes proves nothing. Sam reads the ad and asks who it leaves out.

questions.prompt: The website has only two reviews. A friend says: "Ask the app for ten five-star reviews from happy customers." What should Sam do?

options.text: Post them with first names only, so nobody can ever check who the customers are.
options.explanation: Hiding the names makes it worse, not better. The reviews are still invented, and readers are still misled.

options.text: Post only real reviews, and let the app draft a note that asks real customers for one.
options.explanation: Right. The Anthropic Usage Policy lists fake reviews as a deceptive use. The app can still help with the honest part: a polite request to real customers.

options.text: Post them, but change a few words in each one so they sound like real local people.
options.explanation: Editing the words does not make the customers real. Invented reviews mislead the people who read them.

options.text: Post them for one month only, and delete them all when real reviews come in.
options.explanation: A short time is still a lie to every reader in that month. Fake reviews are deceptive whatever their age.

questions.prompt: The blog draft says: "Vets agree every dog needs exactly two hours of walking a day (Pet Health Study, 2019)." What should Sam do?

options.text: Keep it, because a named study and a year show that the fact was checked.
options.explanation: The Claude Help Center warns that an answer can look authoritative and still not be grounded in fact. A name and a year can be invented too.

options.text: Ask the app to add two more studies, so the point looks stronger to readers.
options.explanation: More sources from the app means more things to check, not more proof. They can be invented in the same way.

options.text: Delete the source line but keep the claim, so nobody asks where it came from.
options.explanation: That hides the problem. The claim is still unchecked, and now readers can't check it either.

options.text: Find the study and read what it says, and cut or reword the claim if it doesn't hold.
options.explanation: Right. The ChatGPT docs say to verify important numbers, names, dates, quotes and claims. If Sam can't find the study, the claim goes.

questions.prompt: The price email said 15 euros a walk. The real price is 25. A customer replies, upset. What should Sam say?

options.text: "Sorry, that mistake is mine. The price is 25. Let's agree a fair deal for this month."
options.explanation: Right. Sam sent the email, so Sam owns the mistake. The ChatGPT docs say a polished response can still be wrong, so review it before you share it. Sam fixes it in the open and checks prices next time.

options.text: "Sorry, an AI app wrote that email for me, so the mistake was not really mine."
options.explanation: The app drafted it, but Sam checked and sent it. Blaming the tool does not fix anything for the customer.

options.text: "The price was always 25 a walk. Please read our website before you book again."
options.explanation: That hides Sam's own mistake and blames the customer. It is not honest.

options.text: "Sorry. From now on I will not use any AI app for my business emails at all."
options.explanation: That does not answer the customer or fix the price. The real fix is to check before sending.
